yātudhāna
(‘one who nourishes the demons’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in the Ṛgveda several times (vide 10.87). It has been employed in the sense of an evil spirit that tries to harm human beings.
Yātudhānas are fond of eating the flesh and drinking the blood of human beings and domestic animals like horses. They can cause serious diseases and even lunacy. They are very active during evenings and nights. They are specially fond of spoiling वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
However, the deity अग्नि is powerful enough to destroy them. Hence prayers are specially offered to him (ibid. 10.87.3, 4, 5, 7).

Yatindramatadīpikā
------------------------------------------
This is the only standard and popular prakaraṇagrantha—elementary textbook—of Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy.
Śrīnivāsadāsa, the author of this treatise, might have lived in the 15th or the 16th century. He was the son of Govindācārya and a disciple of Mahācārya. Being a staunch devotee of Lord वेङ्कटेश, he lived in तिरुपति (in Chittoor district of Andhra Pradesh). Apart from this treatise, he is said to have written a gloss on the Śrutaprakāśikā which itself is a commentary by सुदर्शनसूरि (A.

-1137).
He states that he consulted more than 20 standard books on this subject and has tried to present their summary in an elementary form in this work of his.
This work has one modern commentary called Prakāśa by Vāsudevaśāstri Abhyaṅkar.
The Yatīndramatadīpikā is written in elegant prose and has ten avatāras or chapters.
The first chapter enumerates the different padārthas or categories, first as प्रमाणस् (valid sources of knowledge) and prameyas (objects known through them). It then gives their subdivisions. The theory of सत्ख्याति (‘what is real alone is apprehended’) is established by rejecting other theories like अख्याति and अनिर्वचनीय-ख्याति (See KHYĀTI for details.). The concept of प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception) is explained in detail.
The second chapter deals with अनुमान or inference extensively. Five hetvābhāsas or fallacies of reasoning are explained. Upamiti (analogy) and अर्थापत्ति (implication) are shown to be included in अनुमान itself.
The subject of the third chapter is शब्द pramāṇa or verbal testimony. Apart from establishing that the वेदस् are eternal and have no human author, an attempt is made to prove that all words convey the sense of नारायण, the Supreme Lord.
The fourth chapter is the longest of all. प्रकृति or nature is the main subject matter. The categories of the न्याय school of philosophy are refuted and of the Sāṅkhya school accepted.
The fifth chapter is concerned with kāla or time. It is eternal and all-pervasive. Other aspects of time described are the four युगस्, measurement of ब्रह्मा’s time and life, the periods of मनुस् and Indras as also the refutation of other views regarding time.
The next chapter, the sixth, enumerates the eternal, transcendental attributes of pure सत्त्व (called शुद्धसत्त्व) which belongs both to ईश्वर and जीव. It is of शुद्धसत्त्व that the bodies of ईश्वर, of the muktas or liberated souls and of the world known as वैकुण्ठ are made. At the end there is a nice description of वैकुण्ठ.
The seventh chapter deals with धर्मभूतज्ञान or attributive चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. It is always eternal and and all-pervasive in respect of ईश्वर and the nityas (eternal souls never in bondage). With regard to the bound souls it is contracted or obscured. If and when they attain लिबेरतिओन्, it expands to infinity. Apart from describing the three yogas of कर्म (action), ज्ञान and भक्ति (devotion), the doctrines of भक्ति and प्रपत्ति (self-surrender) are elaborated.
The subject of the eighth chapter is jīvas or individual souls. Common characteristics of the जीव and ईश्वर like self-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् are described first. The true nature of the जीव is then elaborated. There are infinite numbers of jīvas. They are unborn and eternal. They are monadic in size with चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् as the essential nature. Different kinds of jīvas including the liberated ones and their characteristics are described. Views of other schools like that of the Cārvākas and बुद्धिस्म् about the जीव are refuted.
The next chapter—the ninth—is concerned with ईश्वर or God. He is described as the उपादानकारण (material cause), निमित्तकारण (efficient cause) and sahakārikāraṇa (co-operant cause) of the universe. The theory of māyā of the advaitins is refuted. Fivefold aspects of Īśvara—para, vyūha, विभव, अर्चा and antaryāmin—are elaborated.
(See ANTARYĀMIN.)
The tenth and the last chapter explains the adravyas (non-substance) which are ten.
The work concludes by giving a long list of treatises—31 in number—dealing with the Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy from which the essence of this work has been prepared.

Yatidharmasaṅgraha
------------------------------------------
Though the smṛtis and the धर्म-śāstra, as also the पुराणस्, deal with the duties and responsibilities of persons belonging to the four varṇas (castes) and āśramas (stages of life), there are only a few works that deal exclusively with Yatidharma or सṁन्यास. The Yati-dharmasaṅgraha—also known by two more names, the Yatidharmaprakāśa and the Yatidharmasamuccaya—of Viśveśvara-सरस्वती is perhaps the best among such treatises. He was a disciple of Sarvajña-viśveśa and lived earlier than A.

. Nothing more is known about him.
Though the work is in prose, it has profusely quoted from the उपनिषद्स्, the पुराणस् and the smṛtis. Some of them are: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad; Jābāla Upaniṣad; Kaṭha Upaniṣad; Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad; Bhagavadgītā; Viṣṇupurāṇa; Skandapurāṇa; Smṛtis of अत्रि, बृहस्पति, दक्ष, देवल, गोभिल, मनु, पराशर, याज्ञवल्क्य and यम.
The number of topics dealt with exceeds 90.
The more important ones from among them are as follows: when to take सṁन्यास; śrāddhas to be performed; certain rites to be performed by the आहिताग्नि (one who is keeping the Vedic fires) and others who have not; repetition of the praiṣa मन्त्र three times, this being central to the whole process of taking सṁन्यास; accepting the external insignia of सṁन्यास like doraka (girdle), kaupīna (loin-cloth), wearing-cloth, kantha (quilt of rags) and दण्ड (staff); approaching a competent गुरु (preceptor) to acquire आत्मज्ञान (knowledge of the Self); receiving the mahāvākya (great Vedic sentence like tat tvam asi); the few things of necessity that a यति or a saṁnyāsin can keep for the maintenance of the body; code of conduct; service to the गुरु; जप or repetition of प्रणव (Oṁ) and Rudra (a Vedic passage); upāsanā (meditation) on the आत्मन्/Brahman; a saṁnyāsin has no कर्म (rituals) to perform; rules about ablutions, bath and other daily activities; on bhikṣācaryā or begging; how to observe the vows of चातुर्मास्य (ritual staying in a place during the rainy season); method of honouring guest-saṁnyāsins, the processes called paryaṅkavidhi and योग-paṭṭa; things forbidden for a saṁnyāsin; prāyaścittas or expiations for transgressions; mādhukarībhikṣā (collecting alms, even as a bee collects honey, from not more than seven houses); सṁन्यास purifies him and his family; characteristics of a jīvanmukta, the liberated सोउल्.

yati
------------------------------------------
It is one of the terms used to indicate a saṁnyāsin. (See SAṀNYĀSA.)
In prosody it indicates a break in the line, in any metre, to facilitate easy pronunciation.
